sections.title: Every assistant works alone
body: There is an assistant for nearly everything now: one for code, one for research, one for review, often several of each. Each is good at its job, and each lives in its own chat with its own context.
None of them knows what the others are doing. There is no shared plan, no shared memory of the goal, and nothing that checks one assistant’s work against another’s.
sections.caption: Six assistants, six silos.

sections.title: So you become the relay
body: You can make them work together, but only by doing the joining yourself: copying a task from one chat to the next, pasting results back, passing messages along.
Reviews are the weak spot. Each assistant checks its own output, and every gate between steps is you, reading, judging and handing on.
sections.caption: You carry every hand-off and every review.

sections.title: One controller, many contributors
body: Sensei Relay starts by giving each assistant a role. One registers as the controller; the rest register as contributors. They can be different assistants, or several parallel runs of the same one.
The controller owns the goal. Contributors own the tasks they are given. Everyone is connected through Relay rather than through your clipboard.
sections.caption: Registration turns a crowd into a team.

sections.title: Plan, dispatch, report
body: Given a goal, the controller prepares a plan and breaks it into tasks, then distributes them to the contributors that are available.
Each contributor completes its task and reports back to the controller, so progress lives in one place instead of in scrollback across five windows.
sections.caption: Tasks go out along the wires; reports come back.

sections.title: Cross-review, then a metrics gate
body: Results are not self-reviewed. Contributors review each other’s work against the requirement, which catches what a single assistant would wave through.
The controller then consolidates the results and gates them by metrics: requirements covered, tests passing, review score. The goal counts as achieved only when the numbers say so.
sections.caption: Peer checks, one merge, one gate.

sections.title: Built to keep going
body: Real work is messy. Assistants can unregister and register again without the run losing its place, and the controller can hand over to another assistant mid-run.
The goal stays the goal, whoever happens to be holding it.
sections.caption: Leave, rejoin, hand over: the run carries on.

takeaway: Many assistants. One goal. Delivered reliably.
